title: Pull today's cart check log
instruction: Open the daily crash cart checklist before touching the cart.
rationale: The checklist is what turns "the cart looked fine" into a dated record someone can actually be held to — a check that never gets logged is a check nobody downstream can prove happened at all, whether that downstream question comes from a supervisor tomorrow or an inspector months from now.

title: Check the tamper seal before opening
instruction: Confirm the numbered seal on the cart is intact and matches yesterday's log before anything is opened.
rationale: An intact numbered seal is what lets this cart skip a full drawer-by-drawer inventory today — it's the whole reason the seal exists, and a seal that doesn't match yesterday's number means someone opened this cart and it needs the full count regardless of how it looks from outside.

title: Inspect the cart for what the seal alone won't show
instruction: Two things about this cart aren't right, seal or no seal. Find them.
rationale: A seal tells you the cart hasn't been opened since the last check — it doesn't tell you the cart was actually stocked correctly the last time it was closed. This inspection is the check that catches what an intact seal, by itself, never can.

title: Run the defibrillator's self-test
instruction: Start the self-test and read the result before logging the cart ready.
rationale: A defibrillator's own self-test is the one check that actually exercises the device rather than just looking it over — a unit that displays fine on the outside but fails its self-test is a unit that looks ready and isn't, and the only way to tell the difference is running the test itself.

title: Check the cart's portable oxygen level
instruction: Read the portable oxygen tank gauge mounted on the cart.
rationale: The portable tank on this cart is the only oxygen supply that actually moves with it wherever the cart is needed next — a low tank found here, at the daily check, gets swapped out now, not discovered empty in the middle of a response when there's no time left to go looking for a fresh one.

title: Count supplies, then confirm the medication tray
instruction: Count the general supply drawers against the checklist, then confirm the medication tray is present and its own seal is intact.
rationale: General supplies get counted item by item because that's this job's own scope — the medication tray gets checked for its presence and its seal only, because what's inside that tray is pharmacy's count to keep, not this checklist's to open.

title: Reseal the cart with a fresh numbered seal
instruction: Close the cart and apply a new numbered seal, then record the number.
rationale: Tomorrow's whole check depends on today's seal number being written down correctly, not remembered or guessed at — a cart resealed without logging the new number is a cart tomorrow's tech has absolutely no way to verify against anything, seal intact or not.

title: Lock the cart's wheels in its bay
instruction: Engage the wheel locks once the cart is parked in its marked bay.
rationale: A crash cart that can roll is a crash cart that might not be exactly where the next code needs it to be, and a code is not the moment anyone wants to be tracking one down — locked wheels in a marked bay is what makes finding it automatic instead of a search.

title: Sign off today's check
instruction: Record the completed check, the seal number and the time in the log.
rationale: A signed, timed log entry is what lets anyone — a supervisor, an inspector, the next shift picking up where you left off — confirm this cart was actually checked today rather than assumed fine because it usually is, which is exactly the assumption a real emergency has no patience for.

title: Confirm the overhead page
instruction: Repeat the room number and code type back to confirm the page went out correctly.
rationale: An overhead page misheard or relayed wrong sends part of the responding team to the wrong room while the actual room keeps waiting — repeating it back before moving is what catches that mistake in the two seconds it's still fixable, rather than the minute it takes someone to notice they're in the wrong hallway.

title: Hold the hallway clear
instruction: Stand the doorway and keep the path clear for the full response.
rationale: A code team running full speed down a hallway needs that hallway to actually be clear, not clear except for whoever wandered into it — holding the doorway for the whole response is what keeps that path open the entire time it's needed, not just when it happened to be checked.

title: Bring the backup cart to the room
instruction: Roll the sealed backup cart to the doorway the moment the working cart is opened.
rationale: The instant one cart is opened for a code, this floor has zero ready spares until another one arrives — getting the backup cart moving the moment the first one opens is what keeps that gap as short as possible.

title: Direct family to the waiting area
instruction: Walk arriving family members to the designated waiting area, away from the room.
rationale: Family arriving mid-code have nowhere to be that helps and every reason to want to be right at the door — directing them to the waiting area is what keeps the doorway clear and gives them somewhere to actually wait for real information.

title: Restock and reseal the moment the room clears
instruction: Restock everything the code used, then seal the cart with a fresh numbered seal.
rationale: A cart sitting open and half-restocked after a code is a cart with no protection against the next call finding it exactly as depleted as this one left it — restocked and resealed immediately is what makes this cart the next code's ready cart too, not tomorrow's.

title: Log the support tasks and the cart exchange
instruction: Record what was done and the time the working cart was swapped for the backup.
rationale: This log is the only record connecting the cart that responded to this code with the fresh one now sitting in its place — without it, nobody downstream can tell which cart is which or when the swap actually happened.

situation: A family member tries to push past you into the room while the code is still running.
instruction: That gets redirected, not argued with in the doorway.
missed: The family member got past and into the doorway. The one thing this role was holding clear for the code team just stopped being clear.

situation: Another unit on this floor calls saying they need a backup cart right now for a second, unrelated event.
instruction: That's not this room's cart to send.
missed: The half-restocked cart nearly went to the second call instead of the one actually assigned to cover it. Two events were now short a cart each instead of one.

explanation: That equipment is parked square in the path the code team runs down. An egress and response path that's blocked by whatever happened to be convenient to leave there is a blocked path the moment a team actually needs to run it.

That medication tray's seal is already broken and it's just sitting out. A broken seal on a medication tray gets reported to pharmacy and swapped, never opened or counted by anyone whose job is the logistics around it, not what's inside it.

That cart is sitting in the hallway unsealed and unlocked. A crash cart is either sealed and in its bay or it's open because someone's actively using it — parked unsealed in a hallway, it's neither ready nor accounted for.

Those defibrillator pads sitting loose on the cart top are past their date. Pads that have expired don't get left on the cart for whoever opens it next to discover mid-code — they get pulled and swapped the moment the date's checked.

title: Hand hygiene before the line
instruction: Wash hands and glove before touching a ticket or a plate.
rationale: Every tray on this line goes to someone whose immune system may already be working overtime — hand hygiene at the start of the shift is the one habit that protects every ticket that follows it, not just the first one.

title: Pull the ticket and match the room
instruction: Read the tray ticket and confirm the patient's name and room number before assembling anything.
rationale: The ticket is what tells this line which tray is which — building from memory or from where a cart happens to be parked is how a cardiac diet and a regular tray change places without anyone actually deciding it should happen, and the room number on the ticket is the only thing standing between that quiet swap and a tray that reaches the wrong bed looking perfectly correct.

title: Read the ticket for what changes this tray
instruction: Two things on this ticket change what happens next. Find them before you reach for a plate.
rationale: A ticket carries more than what actually changes the build — sorting the flag that redirects this tray from the one that's just charted and routine is the actual skill of reading it, and it happens once, before the first plate comes off the rack.

title: Choose the texture the order calls for
instruction: Match the plate to the ticket's texture order — regular, mechanical soft, or pureed.
rationale: A texture order isn't a preference on the ticket, it's the reason this patient can safely swallow what's on the plate — the wrong texture doesn't taste different or look obviously off, it's a swallowing hazard shaped exactly like an ordinary plate of food, which is exactly why the plate gets matched to the order before anything is served rather than corrected after someone notices.

title: Thicken and cap the ordered beverage
instruction: Mix the thickener to the ticket's consistency, then cap the cup.
rationale: A thickened-liquids order exists because thin liquid moves faster than this patient can safely manage — capping the cup after mixing is what keeps that consistency from being diluted or spilled before it ever reaches the tray.

title: Weigh the portion to the diet order's spec
instruction: Portion the entree and read the scale before it goes on the tray.
rationale: A restricted diet's whole point can be undone by a portion that's simply too large — a renal or cardiac order is written around a specific amount, not a general direction, and the scale is what makes portioning an actual measurement instead of a guess by eye that happens to land close enough most days.

title: Scan the line before you plate
instruction: Two things sitting on this line right now shouldn't go anywhere near a tray. Find them.
rationale: A tray line moves fast enough that a bad utensil or an expired item can end up on a plate simply because it was the closest thing to hand — a quick scan before plating is what catches it while it's still just sitting on the counter, instead of after it's already part of a tray someone is about to eat from.

title: Switch to a dedicated utensil for the allergy tray
instruction: Pick up the clean, dedicated serving tool before touching this ticket's food.
rationale: Once a tray is flagged for an allergy, every tool that touches it has to be one that's never touched the allergen — a shared spoon reused out of convenience is how a flagged tray causes the exact reaction the flag existed to prevent.

title: Marry the ticket to the tray
instruction: Attach the printed ticket to the tray it belongs to before it leaves the line.
rationale: A tray and its ticket separated anywhere between here and the room is a tray nobody downstream can actually verify against anything — clipping them together now, at the one point they're both still in the same hands, is what keeps that verification possible all the way to the bedside instead of just to the cart.

title: Cover the tray for transport
instruction: Lid or cover every plate before the tray goes on the cart.
rationale: A covered plate holds its temperature and stays clear of anything it might pass on its way through the hallway — an elevator, a cart bumped against a doorframe, a cough from someone passing — an uncovered tray is losing both from the moment it leaves the line, not from whenever someone happens to notice.

title: Verify the cart manifest before rolling
instruction: Match every tray's slot to the cart's own manifest before it leaves the kitchen.
rationale: The manifest is what lets the whole cart be trusted at once instead of every tray being checked over again room by room — a tray slotted into the wrong compartment is a tray that reads as delivered correctly right up until the wrong patient actually opens it and finds someone else's diet order on their table.

title: Hold the cart at a safe temperature
instruction: Keep the cart closed and at temperature through the full delivery window.
rationale: A hot-holding cart only protects a tray for as long as it actually stays closed and powered — propped open or unplugged even briefly, the food inside starts sliding out of the range the whole system was built to hold it in.

title: Latch the cart compartment
instruction: Rotate the latch fully closed before moving the cart.
rationale: A latch left half-closed pops open over the first door threshold or elevator gap this cart crosses, and a cart that spills partway down a hallway is a fall hazard as much as it is a ruined delivery — closed and confirmed is what keeps every tray inside where the manifest says it is until it's actually delivered.

title: Check the ID band at the bedside
instruction: Read the patient's ID band against the tray ticket before leaving the tray.
rationale: Everything upstream — the flag, the texture, the thickener, the manifest — was built on the assumption that this tray reaches the right person. The bedside check is the one place that assumption actually gets tested, on the one person it was all built for.

title: Log the delivery
instruction: Record the tray as delivered, refused, or held.
rationale: A tray that's delivered, refused or held all look the same from the kitchen unless someone logs which one happened — that record is what tells the next shift whether this patient actually ate, not just whether a tray left the line.

situation: Someone from the floor calls down asking you to add extra salt packets to this cardiac-diet tray because the patient prefers it that way.
instruction: That request goes back to the order, not straight onto the tray.
missed: Extra salt went on a cardiac-diet tray on a verbal request nobody with authority to change the order actually approved. The tray now contradicts the order it was supposedly built from.

situation: The delivery cart's heating element alarms mid-hold — the temperature is dropping.
instruction: Every tray in that cart needs a working cart, not this one.
missed: The delivery went out on a cart that was already alarming. Every tray riding in it spent the trip sliding further out of a safe holding temperature.

explanation: That thickener packet is past its date. A thickener that doesn't perform to spec doesn't announce itself in the cup — it just leaves a liquid thinner than the order called for, and that's the only warning anyone gets before it's already been swallowed.

That tray is fully built and sitting ready for a room the ticket already marks NPO. A patient held off food and drink for a procedure doesn't get a tray sent up anyway because it happened to already be made — it gets held, not delivered.

That serving spoon just came out of a dish with a tree-nut ingredient in it, and it's sitting on this ticket's tray. A shared utensil carries whatever it last touched onto the next thing it touches — an allergy ticket gets its own tool, not whatever's closest.

That's a regular-texture plate sitting where a pureed order needs to go. Sending regular texture to an order written for pureed is exactly the mismatch a texture-modified diet exists to prevent — a swallowing risk, not a garnish choice.

title: Read the posted precautions before entering
instruction: Check the card on the door for what kind of precautions this room is under.
rationale: The card on the door is what tells you which PPE this room actually needs — contact, droplet or both — before a single glove goes on. Guessing at it from the last room you cleaned is how the wrong barrier goes up on the wrong room.

title: Don PPE to the posted precautions
instruction: Gown first, then gloves pulled up over the gown's cuffs, then eye protection.
rationale: The CDC's transmission-based precautions guidance orders PPE donning for a reason: a gown put on after gloves leaves a gap at the wrist that a glove alone was never meant to cover, and eye protection last means it's the one thing you're not tempted to touch again once your hands are already dirty.

title: Scan the room for what isn't yours to handle
instruction: Two things in this room are for nursing to deal with, not you. Find them before you touch anything else.
rationale: An EVS tech's scope stops at the room, not at every object in it — a sharp or a device left behind by clinical staff gets flagged, not picked up, because handling it wrong is a needlestick this job was never trained for in the first place.

title: Bag the soiled linen without shaking it
instruction: Roll the linen inward on itself and place it straight into the hamper bag.
rationale: Soiled linen carries whatever the patient did, and CDC guidance is explicit that it gets handled with minimum agitation — rolled and bagged, never shaken, snapped or held against the body, because shaking it is how it gets into the air of a room you're trying to clean.

title: Sort regulated waste into the red bag
instruction: Put visibly soiled disposables in the red biohazard bag, not the general trash.
rationale: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard treats anything soaked or caked with blood or other potentially infectious material as regulated waste with its own bag, its own hauler and its own disposal rule — mixing it into general trash turns every bag handler downstream into someone exposed without knowing it.

title: Hold every high-touch surface to its wet-contact time
instruction: Wipe the high-touch surfaces and watch the panel — commit once the surface has stayed visibly wet long enough, per the label.
rationale: A disinfectant only kills what its label says it kills for as long as the surface actually stays wet — that contact time is set by the product's own registered label, not by how fast the wipe feels done, and wiping it dry early means the surface was never actually disinfected at all.

title: Clean the bathroom cleanest surface first
instruction: Wipe the sink and counter, then the toilet — never the other way around.
rationale: Cleaning cleanest-to-dirtiest keeps whatever came off the toilet from ever reaching the counter a patient's hand or toothbrush touches next — reverse the order and the cloth becomes the thing that cross-contaminates the surface you already finished.

title: Reline the emptied bins
instruction: Fit a fresh liner in the trash and the red bag holder before moving on.
rationale: A bin left unlined is a bin the next person in this room reaches for and finds nothing — relining it now is what makes the room actually ready, not just emptied.

title: Take down the soiled privacy curtain
instruction: Unhook the curtain and bag it for laundry rather than leaving it up.
rationale: A privacy curtain gets touched by every hand that passes the bed, and CDC surface guidance treats it the same as any other high-touch item in a precautions room — left up, it carries the last patient's risk straight into the next one's stay.

title: Set the wet floor sign before mopping
instruction: Place the sign at the doorway before the mop touches the floor.
rationale: A wet floor with no sign at the door is a fall waiting on whoever walks in next — the sign goes up before the mop, not after someone has already slipped on a floor they had no way to know was wet.

title: Mop the floor working back to the door
instruction: Work in overlapping strokes from the far corner back toward the door and hold the pass steady.
rationale: Mopping toward the door instead of away from it means you're never standing on floor you haven't cleaned yet, and never re-tracking dirty water back over a section you already finished.

title: Doff PPE in the order that keeps you clean
instruction: Gloves off first, then hand hygiene, then the gown, then the mask or eye protection last.
rationale: The CDC's doffing sequence exists because the most contaminated items come off first and the ones nearest your airway come off last, with a hand-hygiene step between them — skip the order and a hand that just peeled off a soiled glove is the hand about to touch your own face.

title: Log the room and release it
instruction: Mark the room terminally cleaned and release it to bed management.
rationale: Bed management assigns this room to its next patient off this log, not off a guess that the door being open means it's ready — an unlogged room is a room that either sits empty longer than it needs to or gets assigned before it's actually done.

situation: While rolling the linen, something hard and small drops out of the folds onto the floor — it looks like a used syringe cap.
instruction: That is not yours to pick up or dispose of.
missed: The linen bag went to laundry with an unresolved sharp on the floor beside it. Whoever mops that spot next has no idea it's there.

situation: A supply cart passing in the hallway clips the wet floor sign and knocks it flat, right as you're finishing the pass.
instruction: The floor is still wet and the doorway now has no sign standing at it.
missed: The sign stayed down through the rest of the pass. Anyone who walked through that doorway had no warning the floor inside was wet.

explanation: That's the cloth you just used on the toilet, sitting on the sink edge like it's clean. Working dirty to clean instead of clean to dirty puts what came off the toilet onto the next surface a hand actually touches.
That box is exam gloves, and nothing else is on over your uniform yet. Contact precautions are a barrier, not a glove — gloves go on last, over a gown's cuffs, not as the whole outfit.

That bin is unlined general trash, and the wipe in your hand came off a visibly soiled surface. Regulated waste goes in the red bag by the door, not into a bin that ends up in the same truck as the break-room trash.

That sheet is mid-shake. Snapping soiled linen out before it goes in the bag is exactly how whatever is on it gets airborne and lands on a surface you already disinfected — bag it where it lies, don't shake it first.

title: Identify the spill against its own SDS
instruction: Check the spilled item's safety data sheet before doing anything else.
rationale: The SDS is what tells you this is actually a hazardous drug and not something else that happens to look similar — responding to a spill without checking what it actually is means guessing at every decision that follows, from what PPE this calls for to which waste stream it eventually goes in.

title: Restrict the area before anyone gets close
instruction: Set up barriers and keep everyone clear of the spill before PPE even comes out.
rationale: A spill nobody's cordoned off is a spill anyone can walk through, touch, or track further down the hallway without ever knowing it happened — the barrier goes up before the response starts, not once someone's already wandered through the area and carried part of it somewhere else.

title: Don PPE in the order that protects you
instruction: Gown first, then double-glove over the cuffs, then respiratory protection if the spill calls for it.
rationale: USP <800> treats hazardous-drug PPE as a set donned in a specific order for a reason — a gown after gloves leaves a gap at the wrist, and respiratory protection last means it's the one thing you're not tempted to touch again once your gloved hands have already been near the spill.

title: Read the spill against the kit's rated capacity
instruction: Assess the spill's size and confirm it's within what this kit is actually rated to handle.
rationale: Every spill kit is rated for a maximum size in its own instructions — committing to clean up a spill bigger than that rating with a kit that isn't built for it just means running out of absorbent mid-response with contamination still spreading.

title: Absorb the spill with the kit's own pads
instruction: Lay the kit's absorbent pads over the spill from the outside edge in.
rationale: Working from the outside edge in is what keeps the contaminated area from spreading further while it's being absorbed — the kit's own pads are rated for this exact chemistry in a way a generic paper product never is.

title: Collect any fragments with the kit's scoop
instruction: Use the kit's small scoop and forceps to collect broken glass or vial fragments — never by hand.
rationale: A hazardous drug spill that includes broken glass is two hazards stacked in the same footprint — the scoop and forceps in the kit exist so no bare or gloved hand ever has to close around a fragment that's both sharp and contaminated at the same time, in the same motion.

title: Scan for where the spill actually reached
instruction: Two things near this spill are still contaminated and easy to miss. Find them.
rationale: A spill's visible edge is rarely its actual edge — this scan is what catches the linen it soaked into and the trail it left, because a response that stops at the obvious puddle can still leave real contamination sitting a few feet away, waiting for the next person who walks through unaware.

title: Seal everything into the hazardous-drug stream
instruction: Place every absorbent pad, glove, and contaminated item into the hazardous-drug waste bag and seal it.
rationale: Every item this spill touched — pads, gloves, linen, the gown itself — belongs in one dedicated stream, sealed, because a hazardous-drug waste bag with a gap in what it actually contains isn't a contained spill, it's a contained puddle with contaminated items still sitting around it.

title: Clean the surface with detergent and water
instruction: Wash the affected surface with detergent solution after the spill itself is fully absorbed.
rationale: Absorbing the spill removes the bulk of it; the detergent wash is what actually breaks down whatever residue is left behind on the surface itself, which is a genuinely separate step from soaking up the liquid, not a shortcut that happens automatically once the puddle itself is gone.

title: Hold the final decon wipe to its contact time
instruction: Wipe the surface and keep steady, even pressure — not too light, not scrubbing hard enough to spread anything — for the label's full contact time.
rationale: The decontaminating solution's own label sets how long it has to stay in contact with the surface to actually work, and pressure matters too — too light and it barely touches the surface, too hard and you risk spreading residue instead of lifting it.

title: Move the sealed bag to the hazardous-drug bin
instruction: Carry the sealed waste bag to the dedicated hazardous-drug waste container, not the general or regulated one.
rationale: The hazardous-drug bin is tracked and disposed of under its own rule, kept entirely separate from general and regulated medical waste — a bag that ends up in the wrong container is waste that gets handled under a rule that was never written for what it actually contains.

title: Restock the spill kit
instruction: Turn the kit's restock indicator once every component is replaced.
rationale: A spill kit that's been used and never restocked is a kit that looks perfectly ready sitting on its shelf and isn't — turning it back to ready is what makes sure the next spill, whenever and wherever it happens, finds a full kit waiting instead of an empty box with the label still facing out.

title: Doff PPE in the order that keeps you clean
instruction: Outer gloves first, then the gown, then respiratory protection, then the inner gloves last.
rationale: The most contaminated layer comes off first and the layer closest to your bare skin comes off last — reverse that order and a hand that just touched the outside of a contaminated gown is the hand about to touch your own face on the way to removing a respirator.

title: Log the spill incident
instruction: Record what happened, the response taken, and that the area is cleared.
rationale: The log is what turns this response into something the facility can actually review — a pattern of spills in the same spot, a kit that keeps running short, a training gap — none of that is visible to anyone if this incident only exists as something you remember handling.

situation: Once you start absorbing, the spill turns out to have spread further than it first looked — past what this kit is actually rated for.
instruction: This kit doesn't stretch to cover a bigger spill than it's built for.
missed: The response kept going with an undersized kit stretched past its rating. Whatever the kit ran out of partway through is still sitting there, uncontained.

situation: A coworker walks up and leans on the counter right at the edge of the restricted zone, unaware anything happened here.
instruction: The barrier only works if it's actually enforced.
missed: The coworker stayed leaned against the counter, right at the edge of a zone that was supposed to be kept clear. The barrier existed on the floor but not in practice.

explanation: That coffee cup is sitting inside the restricted area. Nothing gets eaten, drunk, or set down open inside a zone that might still carry contamination — it comes out of the area before the response continues, not after someone almost picks it back up.

That's an ordinary roll of paper towels sitting right by the spill. Paper towels don't absorb a hazardous drug spill the way the kit's own pads do, and pushing a spill around with the wrong material just spreads the contaminated area wider.

That's the regular trash bin, sitting closer than the hazardous-drug waste container. Anything that touched this spill goes into the dedicated stream — dropping it in whatever bin happens to be nearest turns ordinary trash into hazardous waste nobody downstream is expecting.

Those are ordinary exam gloves, not the kit's chemo-rated pair. A hazardous drug can permeate an exam glove in a way it can't get through the glove this kit was actually stocked with — the right pair is right next to the wrong one for a reason.

title: Don PPE for the waste room
instruction: Gown, gloves and eye protection before the first bag comes off the chute.
rationale: Everything that reaches this room is contaminated until proven otherwise — OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard treats this job the same as any other exposure risk, because a soiled bag doesn't announce what's actually inside it.

title: Receive bags from the chute
instruction: Pull each bag off the chute landing and stage it for inspection before it moves any further.
rationale: The chute is where every floor's laundry lands in one place, from a routine room change to whatever a code or a fall left behind — staging it here rather than carrying it straight through to the sorters is what gives this room its one real chance to catch a problem bag before it ever reaches the line.

title: Inspect every bag before it moves on
instruction: Two bags on this landing have a problem that gets worse the further they travel. Find them.
rationale: A bag looks the same whether it's fine or failing until somebody actually checks it — this inspection is what catches a leak or an overweight bag while it's still sitting still on the landing, rather than partway down the sorting line where a leak has already spread and an overweight bag has already been lifted.

title: Double-bag the leaking bag
instruction: Contain the leaking bag inside a second bag before it goes anywhere else.
rationale: A second bag around a leaking one is what stops the contamination at this landing instead of on the cart, the floor, or the next person's gloves — it is the whole reason double-bagging exists as a step rather than a suggestion.

title: Sort into the three separate streams
instruction: Place today's waste into the regulated, general and sharps containers, each in its own bin.
rationale: General, regulated and sharps waste are hauled, treated and disposed of under completely different rules — a stream that gets mixed at the sorting stage stays mixed all the way to disposal, which turns a bin of ordinary trash into a bin of regulated medical waste that now has to be treated as one.

title: Weigh the regulated container before sealing
instruction: Read the scale and confirm the container is within its rated weight before you seal it.
rationale: Every regulated waste container has a weight rating set by its own manufacturer — a container sealed over that limit is a container that can split, buckle or fail exactly where a hauler has to lift and stack it, and a failure at that point spreads whatever the container was holding across a dock full of other people's loads.

title: Seal the container and complete the manifest
instruction: Seal the lid and fill in the manifest tag before the container leaves this room.
rationale: The manifest is what makes this container's contents, weight and origin something the hauler and the facility can both be held to later — a container that leaves without one is untraceable the moment it's out the door, and untraceable is exactly the state regulated waste is never supposed to reach.

title: Scan the staging area before loading
instruction: Two containers on this dock aren't ready to go out. Find them.
rationale: The dock is the last place anything gets caught before it becomes the hauler's problem instead of this room's — a scan here, right before loading, is what keeps a labelling gap or an overfilled bin from riding out the door unnoticed and turning into someone else's discovery later.

title: Respond to the spill with its kit
instruction: Apply the spill kit's absorbent and hold the containment steady through the full cleanup.
rationale: A body-fluid spill kit is built to be used start to finish in one motion — absorbent down, contained, disposed of as regulated waste — and stopping partway through leaves exactly the kind of half-contained spill the kit exists to prevent.

title: Move the sealed container to the dock
instruction: Roll the sealed, manifested container to its marked slot on the loading dock.
rationale: The dock slot is where the hauler expects to find exactly what the manifest describes, in the order the pickup route runs — a container parked anywhere else, even a few feet away, is a container the pickup can miss entirely and this room has to explain going nowhere on the manifest that says it left.

title: Run the cart washer
instruction: Turn the wash valve and run the empty linen cart through its full cycle.
rationale: An empty cart still carries whatever it was hauling right up until it's actually washed, not just emptied out — running it through the washer before it goes anywhere near the clean bay is what keeps yesterday's soiled load off today's clean linen instead of just out of sight.

title: Release the cart once it's dry
instruction: Confirm the washed cart is fully dry before releasing it to the clean bay.
rationale: A cart released wet carries moisture into a clean linen load the same way a soiled one carries contamination — dry and actually confirmed is the real bar for clean here, not just recently run through the washer and pushed straight back into service.

title: Restock the clean linen supply
instruction: Unload today's delivery and shelve it on the clean linen rack.
rationale: A floor that runs out of clean linen mid-shift reaches for whatever's closest, which is exactly how corners get cut elsewhere in the building — keeping this shelf actually stocked, unloaded and shelved rather than left sitting on a pallet by the door, is what keeps that pressure from building up in the first place.

title: Log the pickup and the shift's count
instruction: Record the hauler's pickup and today's container count in the log.
rationale: The log is what lets this facility answer, months later, exactly how much regulated waste left the building on a given day and who signed it out — a shift that isn't logged is a shift regulators and auditors alike have no record of.

situation: A bag turns up on the sorting line with no colour coding and no label at all — it could be general or it could be regulated.
instruction: That doesn't get guessed at.
missed: The unlabeled bag went into general waste on a guess. If it was actually regulated, every bag it touched on the way there now has the same question hanging over it.

situation: While you're still finishing the first cleanup, a second spill is spotted a few feet away.
instruction: One kit, one spill at a time — this one needs another set of hands.
missed: Both spills got worked at once, alone. Neither one actually got the kit's full, uninterrupted process, which is the only way either one counts as contained.

explanation: Those boxes are stacked right across the spill kit station. The one time this kit actually matters is the one time nobody can afford to dig it out from behind a pallet — it stays clear, always.

That cart came straight off a soiled run and it's parked in the clean bay. A soiled cart in the clean bay contaminates every clean linen load that touches that space next, which defeats the entire reason the two bays are kept apart.

That yellow hazardous-drug container has ordinary food wrapper and general trash sitting in it. Mixing anything into a dedicated stream doesn't just contaminate that bin — it turns everything else in it into the same problem the label was written to contain.

There's a sharp visibly poking through that bag, and a bare-handed squeeze is exactly what's about to happen to it. A bag that shows a sharp through the plastic gets set down and handled with the tool built for it, never compressed or squeezed by hand to make it fit.

title: Verify the ID band against the transport ticket
instruction: Read the patient's ID band and match it to the name and destination on the ticket.
rationale: A transport ticket sends the right equipment to the right room, but only the ID band on the patient's own wrist confirms this is actually the person that ticket is for — moving the wrong patient is a mistake this one check exists to catch before it starts.

title: Lock the brakes before the transfer
instruction: Set both wheel brakes on the wheelchair before the patient stands.
rationale: A wheelchair that rolls even a few centimeters while someone is mid-stand is how a controlled transfer becomes a fall — the brakes get checked and locked before anyone puts weight on the footrests or the seat.

title: Check the transport oxygen tank before disconnecting wall O2
instruction: Read the tank gauge and confirm it's in the safe range for the trip before switching over.
rationale: A transport tank has to carry enough for the trip plus a margin, per its own gauge — switching over on a tank you haven't actually read is how a patient on oxygen ends up between floors with none.

title: Transfer with a gait belt, not a solo lift
instruction: Apply the gait belt, stand and pivot together, then seat the patient in the wheelchair.
rationale: The gait belt gives the transport tech a secure hold on the patient's center of gravity instead of an arm or a gown — paired with a second set of hands, it's what turns a stand-and-pivot into a controlled movement instead of a lift either person is doing alone.

title: Apply the fall-risk indicator already on the chart
instruction: Check the chart's fall-risk flag and clip on the matching yellow band before the trip starts.
rationale: The flag is already on the chart — this step is carrying it through, not deciding it. Every unit this patient passes through reads that band on sight, which is the whole point of it following the patient rather than staying on a door nobody's near anymore.

title: Scan the room before you move
instruction: Two things in this room will cause a problem the second this chair starts moving. Find them.
rationale: A trip that starts smoothly and snags on the doorway thirty seconds later is not a trip that started safely — the room gets checked for exactly this kind of thing before the wheels ever turn, not fixed on the fly once something's already caught.

title: Deploy the footrests for the ride
instruction: Swing the footrests back into position and confirm they're locked.
rationale: Footrests folded up for the transfer go back down and lock before the chair moves anywhere — a foot dragging along the floor the whole trip is its own injury, separate from the one the transfer itself was built to avoid.

title: Hold the elevator door while boarding
instruction: Press and hold the door-open control while the chair rolls fully inside.
rationale: A standard elevator door's timer is built for someone walking through empty-handed, not a wheelchair, an IV pole and a tech backing it in — holding the door open is what keeps it from closing on the equipment or the patient mid-load.

title: Position the equipment foot-end first
instruction: Load the wheelchair so the patient faces the doors, per the building's own transport convention.
rationale: This building's transport routing is written the same way for every crew so nobody has to work out chair orientation fresh on every ride — following it here is what keeps the patient facing out, clear of the closing doors, and the tech in control of the chair the whole ride.

title: Hand off to the receiving unit
instruction: Give the receiving staff a verbal report, then update the tracking log with the patient's new location.
rationale: A ticket dropped at a desk tells nobody anything until someone happens to read it — a verbal handoff means the receiving unit knows this patient arrived the moment they actually did, and the tracking log is what lets the next person who needs to find this patient actually do it.

title: Lock the brakes again at the destination
instruction: Set the brakes before this patient transfers out of the chair.
rationale: The brakes get set fresh at every stop this trip makes — the ones locked back at the first room mean nothing to a chair that's been rolled, turned and ridden in an elevator since then.

title: Slide-board the patient to the bed
instruction: Bridge the board between the chair and the bed and hold a steady, controlled slide.
rationale: A slide board lets the patient's weight move across a smooth bridge instead of being lifted by hand — holding the slide steady rather than rushing it is what keeps the board from shifting out from under the patient halfway across.

title: Return the equipment to its dock
instruction: Wheel the chair back to its charging dock and plug it in.
rationale: Equipment left wherever the last trip ended is equipment the next trip can't find charged and ready — docking it now is what makes the next tech's trip start on time instead of hunting the floor for a working chair.

title: Log the trip complete
instruction: Close out the transport ticket in the system.
rationale: An open ticket reads as a patient still in transit — closing it the moment the trip actually ends is what keeps the tracking board honest for whoever's watching it for the next request.

situation: Right after standing, the patient says they feel dizzy and unsteady.
instruction: That gets reported before this trip continues, not noted for later.
missed: The trip continued with an unreported dizzy spell on the record nowhere. Whatever caused it is now travelling with the patient instead of being looked at where it happened.

situation: Partway across the slide board, the receiving bed rolls slightly — its brake was never set.
instruction: The slide stops until the bed is actually secured.
missed: The transfer finished across a bed that was never actually secured. The gap between the board and a bed that can still move is exactly where a patient ends up on the floor instead of on the mattress.

explanation: That gurney is parked across the fire exit while you finish up. An egress path blocked even for a few minutes is a hazard for everyone on this floor, not just an inconvenience for whoever needs it next.

That transport oxygen tank's inspection tag is expired. A tank that hasn't been checked on schedule is not the one you grab for a patient who needs oxygen during the trip — pull a current one instead.

That's a one-person lift on a patient who needs a gait belt and a second set of hands. Safe patient handling exists because a solo manual lift is exactly the motion that puts a career-ending back injury on the transport tech and the patient both — not because it's slower to ask for help.

That wheelchair is standing on a ramp with its brakes off. An unlocked chair on any grade rolls the moment weight shifts onto it — brakes get set before anyone reaches for the seat, every time, ramp or flat floor.

title: Don decontamination PPE
instruction: Fluid-resistant gown, gloves to the elbow, mask and full face or eye protection before the case cart is opened.
rationale: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard treats the decontamination area as a splash zone — a washer's spray arms and a manual pre-soak both throw contaminated fluid, and PPE rated for that is what stands between this job and a mucous-membrane exposure nobody saw coming.

title: Receive the case cart on the dirty side only
instruction: Log the case cart in at the decontamination intake, never past the line into the clean assembly area.
rationale: The dirty side and the clean side of this department exist because nothing contaminated is allowed to cross back over a clean surface — every tray in this cart is treated as contaminated until it has been all the way through the line.

title: Disassemble and open before cleaning
instruction: Take multi-part instruments apart and open every hinge and box lock fully.
rationale: A hinge closed during cleaning is a hinge the washer's spray never actually reaches — CDC guidance is explicit that instruments are cleaned open and disassembled, because a closed box lock hides exactly the debris a closed inspection would miss too.

title: Check for bioburden a washer alone won't clear
instruction: Two instruments on this tray need attention before they go anywhere near the washer. Find them.
rationale: A washer-disinfector cleans what water and enzymatic detergent can reach — gross bioburden in a hinge or a blocked lumen needs a hand and a brush first, because a machine cycle run over debris this size does not remove it, it just wets it.

title: Pre-soak lumened and hinged instruments
instruction: Soak and manually brush lumened and hinged instruments in enzymatic solution mixed to the label's dilution, for the label's soak time.
rationale: Enzymatic detergent breaks down protein bioburden before it dries any harder onto the instrument, and its dilution and soak time are set by its own label — too weak or too short and it's done nothing; the point is contact, per the label, not a quick dip.

title: Load and run the washer-disinfector
instruction: Rack the trays open-side down and hold the load through the full washer cycle.
rationale: A washer-disinfector cycle is validated as a whole — spray pattern, detergent, temperature and time together — and opening the door partway through means none of it ran for as long as this load needed.

title: Verify the washer-disinfector's cycle parameters
instruction: Read the cycle's printed temperature and commit once it's within the machine's own validated range.
rationale: The washer's manufacturer instructions for use set the temperature and time the cycle has to actually reach for the mechanical wash to count — a cycle that finished without ever reaching that reading washed nothing, whatever the door light says.

title: Pass the clean tray to the assembly side
instruction: Move the washed, dried tray through the pass-through window onto the assembly bench.
rationale: The pass-through window is the one controlled crossing between the dirty and clean sides — a tray only moves through it once it's actually washed and dried, never carried around the line by hand.

title: Count the tray against its count sheet
instruction: Verify every instrument's type and quantity against the tray's own count sheet.
rationale: A missing instrument found in this room is a missing instrument; a missing instrument found in a patient later is a retained surgical item — the count sheet is what catches the gap here, on the bench, instead of in the OR.

title: Function-test every instrument before it's packaged
instruction: Two instruments on this tray are damaged, not dirty. Find them before assembly.
rationale: A washer and a sterilizer both act on whatever instrument is in front of them — neither one checks whether the instrument still works, which is why every piece gets looked at and tested by hand before it goes back into a tray.

title: Assemble the tray to its count sheet
instruction: Line the tray, arrange every instrument in the layout the count sheet shows, then place the internal indicator.
rationale: The layout on the count sheet exists so the surgical team can see at a glance that everything is present and undamaged the moment the tray opens — a tray assembled any other way makes the OR do the counting work all over again under time pressure.

title: Latch the rigid sterilization container
instruction: Rotate the latch fully closed and confirm the seal.
rationale: A rigid container only keeps its contents sterile if its filter and gasket seal is actually engaged — a latch left half-turned looks closed but leaves a gap steam can get through on the way in and contamination can get through on the way out.

title: Run the sterilizer cycle
instruction: Start the cycle and stay with it until the chamber cycles through on its own.
rationale: Steam sterilization works by combining three numbers over the same span of minutes, not any one of them alone — a door popped open early trims all three at once, so the exposure this tray gets is whatever the shortened run happened to reach, not what the cycle was built to deliver.

title: Read the sterilizer's printout
instruction: Match the printed numbers against the sterilizer's posted spec before you sign off on this load.
rationale: AAMI ST79 makes the paper strip, not the indicator light, the record a load's release rests on — a chamber can flash "cycle complete" after a run that stalled below temperature the whole way through, and only the printed trace would ever show that.

title: Run the biological indicator and log the load
instruction: Run the biological indicator with its matched control, then close out the load record.
rationale: A chemical indicator only shows the chamber reached conditions; the spore strip is what actually gets exposed to those conditions and either dies or doesn't, and its matched control is the reason a clean result means the spores were alive to begin with rather than dead in the vial before the cycle ever ran. None of that protects a soul, though, until it's written down against a tray someone can find again.

situation: The OR calls down: a case is starting and someone's asking if this tray can be rushed through on immediate-use sterilization instead of the normal line.
instruction: That is not a call to make alone at this bench.
missed: A rushed tray went up without anyone with the authority to approve it actually signing off. Every step it skipped between here and the OR is now riding on a case already in progress.

situation: The sterilizer throws a fault code and stops mid-cycle. The door stays locked.
instruction: Nothing inside that chamber right now counts as sterile.
missed: The faulted load sat behind a locked door with nobody logging what happened. Whoever opens that chamber next has no way to tell a stopped cycle from a finished one just by looking.

explanation: That case cart is parked touching the clean assembly bench. The whole point of a decontamination area and a clean assembly area is that nothing contaminated ever touches a surface on the clean side — park it back on the dirty side before anything else moves.

That control skips straight to an immediate-use cycle on a tray that hasn't even been counted yet. Immediate-use steam sterilization is an exception for a specific, unplanned need, not a shortcut around decontamination and assembly whenever someone's in a hurry — and it is never a call this bench makes alone.

That tray on the clean side has no count sheet and no tracking label on it. An unlabeled tray can't be matched to the case it's going to or the cycle that's supposed to sterilize it — it's untraceable the moment it leaves this bench.

That pouch is stuffed and bulging around the tray inside it. A wrap or pouch has to fit the load without crushing the pack — steam needs room to reach every surface, and a pack this crushed hasn't got it.

title: Confirm the exit path before the shift
instruction: Check that the desk's own path to the exit is clear before the first visitor arrives.
rationale: A clear path costs nothing to check at the start of a quiet shift and everything to discover blocked in the middle of a tense one — this gets confirmed before the desk opens, not rediscovered when it's already needed.

title: Check the duress radio's battery
instruction: Read the radio's battery level before clipping it on for the shift.
rationale: A duress radio that dies partway through a shift is a silent alarm with nobody listening — checking the charge now is what keeps that radio actually able to reach security the one time it matters.

title: Test the duress button
instruction: Press the daily test sequence on the desk's duress button and confirm it registers.
rationale: 8 CCR 3342 treats a proven alarm as part of the written plan, not an assumption — a button tested daily is a button this desk can actually trust in the one moment it's ever pressed for real.

title: Scan the lobby before opening the desk
instruction: Two things in this lobby aren't right for the start of a shift. Find them.
rationale: The hazard walk 8 CCR 3342 calls for is exactly this: a look around before anything happens, catching what's wrong with the room while there's still time to fix it rather than during the one moment the room's condition actually matters.

title: Confirm the visitor sign-in system
instruction: Check that the visitor log and badge system are actually working before the lobby fills up.
rationale: A sign-in system that's down is a lobby with no record of who's actually in the building — confirming it works now is what keeps that record honest for the whole shift instead of just for whoever happened to sign in after someone noticed the problem.

title: Notice the cues, then put distance between you
instruction: Notice the raised voice and pacing, then reposition behind the counter before saying anything else.
rationale: A raised voice and pacing are behaviors, not a diagnosis this desk is ever making — noticing them early is what buys the time to reposition behind the counter before things escalate further, rather than reacting to a problem that's already right in front of you.

title: Try the calm approach first
instruction: Lower your own tone, acknowledge the concern out loud, then offer a concrete choice.
rationale: A slower, lower voice is the one thing in this exchange this desk actually controls, and it tends to pull the other person's pace down with it — acknowledging the concern before offering a choice is what makes the choice sound like an option instead of a dismissal.

title: Use the duress button
instruction: Press and hold the button once the calm approach isn't working.
rationale: The duress button alerts security silently, without announcing anything to the visitor at all — holding it the full count is what actually completes the alert rather than a half-press that registers as nothing on the other end.

title: Slide the closed sign into the window
instruction: Move the temporarily-closed sign into the desk window while security is on the way.
rationale: Redirecting the next arrivals away from an active incident, quietly, is what keeps this from turning into a room full of people walking straight into it — the sign does that without announcing anything to the visitor still at the counter.

title: Secure the back office door
instruction: Turn the lock and confirm the back office is sealed.
rationale: The back office is where this desk actually retreats to if the situation gets worse — a door that isn't locked and confirmed isn't a secure room, it's just a room that happens to have a door.

title: Move other visitors clear
instruction: Direct waiting visitors away from the desk and toward the far side of the lobby.
rationale: Everyone else in this lobby is a bystander to whatever's happening at the desk, not part of it — moving them clear is what keeps a two-person situation from turning into a crowd around it.

title: Confirm security is responding
instruction: Follow up on the duress alert to confirm security actually heard it and is on the way.
rationale: A duress signal sent is not the same as a duress signal received — confirming security is actually responding is what turns "I pressed the button" into "help is coming," which is the only version of this that actually matters.

title: Log the incident and ask for a debrief
instruction: Complete the violent-incident log, then request a debrief for yourself.
rationale: The incident log is what 8 CCR 3342 turns into the next hazard correction, but it says nothing about the person who was actually standing at that desk — requesting a debrief is what puts that on the record too, not as an afterthought but as its own line.

situation: A second person nearby starts filming and shouting encouragement at the visitor instead of stepping back.
instruction: That bystander needs moving too, not engaging with.
missed: The bystander kept filming and shouting the whole time, unaddressed. What started as one tense visitor now has an audience actively encouraging it.

situation: Someone pounds on the locked back office door claiming to be an off-duty nurse who needs in right now.
instruction: A claim through a locked door doesn't verify itself.
missed: The door got answered on a claim nobody actually verified. Whatever the room was locked to keep out just walked back in because it sounded urgent enough.

explanation: That card says "you need to calm down right now." Telling an already escalating person to calm down is an order, not de-escalation, and an order is exactly the kind of thing that pushes a tense visitor further rather than defusing anything.

This duress-button test log hasn't been signed in days. An untested button that everyone assumes still works is worse than no button at all, because nobody finds out it's dead until the moment they actually need it.

Those zip ties are sitting on the desk like a tool for this job. Physically restraining a visitor is never this desk's role, whatever's happening — that's what security and, if it comes to it, law enforcement are for, not a clerk reaching for something to hold someone with.

That's the door to the secure back office, propped open with a wedge. Every lockdown control this desk has depends on that door actually closing when it needs to — propped open, it's not a secure room, it's just a room.
